notes.text: Sat — That is, was settled in the house which Hiram's men had built for him, then he reflected upon the unsettled state of the ark.
Curtains — That is, in a tent or tabernacle, ver. 6, composed of several curtains.

Nathan said — Pursue thy intentions, and build an house for the ark. The design being pious and the thing not forbidden by God, Nathan hastily approves it, before he had consulted God about it, as both he and David ought to have done in a matter of so great moment. And therefore Nathan meets with this rebuke, that he is forced to acknowledge his error, and recant it. For the holy prophets did not speak all things by prophetic inspiration, but some things by an human spirit.
The word of the Lord came — Because David's mistake was pious, and from an honest mind, God would not suffer him to lie long in it.
Shalt thou — That is, thou shalt not.
Tent and tabernacle — These two seem thus to be distinguished, the one may note the curtains and hangings within, the other the frame of boards, and coverings upon it.

My servant — Lest David should be too much discouraged, or judge himself neglected of God, as one thought unworthy of so great an honour, God here gives him the honourable title of his servant, thereby signifying that he accepted of his service, and good intentions.

Appoint — That is, I will make room for them, whereas hitherto they have been much distressed by their enemies. Or, I will establish a place for them, that is, I will establish them in their place or land. My people - Among the favours which God had vouchsafed, and would vouchsafe to David, he reckons his blessings to Israel, because they were great blessings to David; partly, because the strength and happiness of a king consists in the multitude and happiness of his people; and partly, because David was a man of a public spirit, and therefore no less affected with Israel's felicity than with his own. Before time - Namely in Egypt.

And as since — Nor as they did under the Judges. But all this is to be understood with a condition, except they should notoriously forsake God. And have caused thee - That is, and as until this time in which I have given thee rest. But these words, though according to our translation they be enclosed in the same parenthesis with the foregoing clauses, may be better put without it, and taken by themselves. For the foregoing words in this verse, and in ver. 10, all concern the people of Israel; but these words concern David alone, to whom the speechs returns after a short digression concerning the people of Israel. And they may be rendered thus. And I will cause thee to rest, &c. - More fully and perfectly than yet thou dost. He will, &c. - For thy good intentions to make him an house, he will make thee an house, a sure house, that is, he will increase and uphold thy posterity, and continue thy kingdom in thy family.

And when, &c. — When the time of thy life shall expire. This phrase implies, that his days shall be prolonged to the usual course of nature, and not cut off in the midst, by any violent or untimely death. I will set - I will set up in thy throne, thy posterity, first Solomon, and then others successively, and at last the Messiah. So the following words may be understood, part of his posterity in general, part of Solomon, and part of Christ only, according to the different nature of the several passages.

He shall — This is meant literally of Solomon, who alone did build the material house or temple; but ultimately of Christ, who is the builder of God's spiritual house or temple. For my name - That is, for my service, and glory. For ever - This is not meant of Solomon, for his kingdom was not forever. But it is to be understood of David's posterity, in general, and with special respect to Christ, in whose person the kingdom was to be lodged forever. 14. His father - I will carry myself towards him as a father, with all affection, and I will own him as my son. This is intended both of Solomon, as a type of Christ; and of Christ himself as is evident from Heb. i, 5. If he commit - This agrees only to Solomon and some others of David's posterity; but not to Christ, who never committed iniquity, as Solomon did, who therein was no type of Christ, and therefore this branch is terminated in Solomon; whereas in those things wherein Solomon was a type of Christ, the sense passes through Solomon to Christ. Rod of men - With such rods as are gentle and moderate, and suited to man's weakness.

glossa.text:
*All that is in thy heart, go and do. ((RAB. in lib. Reg., tom. III.))* It is plain that the spirit of prophecy does not always irradiate the minds of the prophets. *For the Spirit breatheth where he will ((Joan. III))*. Hence Eliseus says: *The Lord hath hid it from me, and hath not told me ((IV Reg. IV))*. Which God disposes out of the dispensation of his loving-kindness: because, while he gives and withdraws the spirit of prophecy, he lifts up the minds of those who prophesy on high, and keeps them in humility, so that, receiving the spirit, they may find what they are of God, and again, not having the spirit of prophecy, they may know what they are of themselves.

((GREG., lib. VII Moral., cap. 17.)) A man ought to be clean in himself from vices, etc., *as far as* he must needs blush to instruct the minds of his neighbours.
*Shalt thou.* ((RAB.)) Another translation, etc., *as far as* he shall build me a house.
*And I will appoint a place.* He describes the time of Solomon, in which the children of Israel had peace on every side, and were not afflicted as in the time of the Judges.

notes.text: Exact — Not conquer him or make him tributary.

Set — Establish his power and dominion. The sea - The mid- land sea. The rivers - Euphrates, called rivers, in regard of divers branches of it, and rivers which flow into it. So here is a description of the uttermost bounds of the promised land.

My first-born — As he calls me father, ver. 26, so I will make him my son, yea my first-born; who had divers privileges above other sons. This and the following passage in some sort agree to David, but are properly accomplished in Christ. Higher - This also was in some sort accomplished in David, but more fully in the Messiah.
For ever — To sit upon the throne forever, as the next words explain it. This was accomplished only in Christ.
A witness — The rainbow, which is God's faithful witness, a token of God's everlasting covenant between God and every living creature for perpetual generations, Gen. ix, 12, 16.

glossa.text: *David my servant, with my holy oil I have anointed him.* ((AUG.)) Strong of hand, an obedient servant, therefore in him I have placed help.

*The enemy in him.* ((ID.)) The devil, whence: *The prince of this world cometh, and in me he hath not anything ((Joan. XIV))*.

*The son of iniquity shall not go on to hurt.* Judas shall not go on, shall not add the effect to the will.
*From his face his enemies.* ((AUG.)) When his face looks upon sinners, they are separated from crimes, for which there is no place under his presence.
*And my truth and my mercy shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted.* ((ID.)) Often mercy and truth are commended to us, etc., *as far as* where these meet one another.
*But if they forsake.* Not only concerning those who persist, but also concerning those who fall, do I promise these things.

*With a rod.* For who is a son? etc., *as far as: And with stripes,* etc.

*I will not scatter.* ((AUG.)) He himself does not take away his mercy from him who is indeed a Christian: but if a man is so wicked that he flees when his father draws near, he alienates himself, the father does not cast him off.

*Neither will I profane.* The promise would be profane, if it were unfulfilled. Is nothing sent into the vessels out of that net because of the bad fishes? The good fishes shall surely be sent, that is, those whom he has predestinated.

*I have sworn once.* ((CASS.)) Man swears often, God *once,* who is not changed.

*In the holy one.* In the man Christ, in whom was to be fulfilled what I have sworn; or David, that is Christ, through holiness. *The seed,* Christians.

*As the sun in the sight.* ((AUG.)) According to the soul, etc., *as far as* in heaven, that is, Christ.

*But thou hast rejected.* ((CASS.)) Diapsalma. Fourthly he sets adverse things against the promises aforesaid, lest they be thought to be fulfilled in another than in the Christ who was then to come. *But thou hast rejected.* As if to say, these goods are for Christians, but not for the Jews, who have deprived themselves of the promise, and this is it: But thou hast rejected *thy Christ,* that is, David the anointed, from the kingdom for the sin which he committed against Urias concerning Bethsabee; *And thou hast despised,* or *hast spurned,* because he suffered many unworthy things; *thou hast deferred,* long in tribulation, *the testament,* the things promised to the Jews, they have been carried over to the Gentiles. ((AUG.)) *But thou.* Or, all these things concerning Christ and the Church: *thou hast rejected* to the gibbet *thy Christ,* and hast given him over to contempt. Or, thou hast deferred him from glory, for a time, or according to his members.

notes.text: Wherefore remember — Such a remembrance strengthens faith, and increases gratitude. That ye being formerly gentiles in the flesh - Neither circumcised in body nor in spirit. Who were accordingly called the uncircumcision - By way of reproach. By that which is called the circumcision - By those who call themselves the circumcised, and think this a proof that they are the people of God; and who indeed have that outward circumcision which is performed by hands in the flesh.

Were at that time without Christ — Having no faith in, or knowledge of, him. Being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel - Both as to their temporal privileges and spiritual blessings. And strangers to the covenants of promise - The great promise in both the Jewish and Christian covenant was the Messiah. Having no hope - Because they had no promise whereon to ground their hope. And being without God - Wholly ignorant of the true God, and so in effect atheists. Such in truth are, more or less, all men, in all ages, till they know God by the teaching of his own Spirit. In the world - The wide, vain world, wherein ye wandered up and down, unholy and unhappy.
Far off — From God and his people. Nigh - Intimately united to both.

For he is our peace — Not only as he purchased it, but as he is the very bond and center of union. He who hath made both - Jews and gentiles, one church. The apostle describes,

1. The conjunction of the gentiles with Israel, ver. 14, 15. And,

2. The conjunction of both with God, ver. 15-18. Each description is subdivided into two parts. And the former part of the one, concerning abolishing the enmity, answers the former part of the other; the latter part of the one, concerning the evangelical decrees, the latter part of the other. And hath broken down the middle wall of partition - Alluding to that wall of old, which separated the court of Israel from the court of the gentiles. Such a wall was the ceremonial law, which Christ had now taken away.

15. Having abolished by his suffering in the flesh the cause of enmity between the Jews and gentiles, even the law of ceremonial commandments, through his decrees - Which offer mercy to all; see Colossians ii, 14. That he might form the two - Jew and gentile. Into one new man - one mystical body.
In one body — One church. Having slain - By his own death on the cross. The enmity - Which had been between sinners and God.

And he came — After his resurrection. And preached peace - By his ministers and his Spirit. To you - Gentiles. That were afar off - At the utmost distance from God. And to them that were nigh - To the Jews, who were comparatively nigh, being his visible church.

For through him, we both — Jews and gentiles. Have access - Liberty of approaching, by the guidance and aid of one Spirit to God as our Father. Christ, the Spirit, and the Father, the three-one God, stand frequently in the same order.
Therefore ye are no longer strangers, but citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem; no longer foreigners, but received into the very family of God.

And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets — As the foundation sustains the building, so the word of God, declared by the apostles and prophets, sustains the faith of all believers. God laid the foundation by them; but Christ himself is the chief corner-stone of the foundation. Elsewhere he is termed the foundation itself, 1 Cor. iii, 11.

On whom all the building fitly framed together — The whole fabric of the universal church rises up like a great pile of living materials. Into an holy temple in the Lord - Dedicated to Christ, and inhabited by him, in which he displays his presence, and is worshipped and glorified. What is the temple of Diana of the Ephesians, whom ye formerly worshipped, to this?

glossa.text: *For which cause.* That you may know that all things are from the grace of God. He had compared the Jews and the Gentiles, in that both had been under sin, now he shows that the Gentiles were the more unworthy and had endured the reproaches of the Jews, so that, being now equal to the Jews, they may be the more beholden to the grace of God. *Sometime you.* In certain codices it is found to be written: *who,* in this place: *you who were Gentiles,* and according to this it is read suspensively as far as this place: *Now, however, in Christ,* etc.; the sense nevertheless remaining the same.

*Strangers.* Hospes, as it were ostii pes, the foot of the door, because when one was received into a house, the master of the house, and he who was received, set his foot upon the doorway, and, right hands having been given, he swore that his entry was peaceable.

*Who hath made both one.* For he himself is the corner stone, in whom two peoples, as walls coming to one another from a different angle, are joined as it were in the kiss of peace. *The wall.* That is, the obstacle, on this side from the law, on that side from idolatry.

*Making peace,* etc. He makes peace between them, that he may reconcile both to God the Father. *In himself.* Not otherwise than by the cross, that is, by death, did he slay the enmity which was between God and men, that is, he forgave sins. For the death of the Saviour profited all.
*You were far off,* etc. If thou lovest God with affection, thou art near: if thou hatest, thou art far off. For it is not by regions that anyone is far from God, but by affections.

*You are not strangers.* That is, less worthy in the faith, as those formerly received under the law. *And sojourners.* That is, foreign to God. *But you are fellow citizens.* That is, of the same right and dignity in the house of God. *Of the saints.* Not of carnal Israel. *And the domestics.* That is, of the household. *Of God.* To whom he reveals secrets.

*He himself the chief corner stone,* etc. ((AUG., in Psal. LXXXVI.)) Lest the Apostles or the prophets (in whom the city is founded) should hold to themselves, following on he says in himself: *He himself the chief corner stone, Christ Jesus;* for indeed the whole building rests upon Christ as upon the first foundation: which foundation is at the top, not at the bottom, as in a bodily structure.
*It groweth into a holy temple in the Lord.* No one is so perfect that he cannot grow.

notes.text: Luke ix, 10.
Matt. xiv, 13; John vi, 1.
They departed — Across a creek or corner of the lake.
Coming out — of the vessel.

glossa.text:
*And gathering together. ((HIER.))* To the place whence the rivers go out they return. They always render thanks to God for those things which they have received.

*All things.* The apostles report to the Lord not only what they themselves had done and taught, but also what John suffered while they were teaching. Either his own disciples, or those of the same John, as Matthew writes.

*Come apart. ((BEDA.))* Not only for the sake of a seeking again, but mystically it signifies that, Judaea being left, which, etc., *as far as* he comes apart, he leads those whom he chooses, that among men living ill they may not attend to evil things, as Lot in Sodom, and Job in the land of Hus, and Abdias in the house of Achab.

*Rest ye.* As the birds in the branches of the mustard. Little is the rest here for the saints, long the labour: but afterwards it is said to them that they should rest from their labours.

*For there were,* etc. ((HIER.)) In the ark of Noe the animals that were within were sent forth, and those that were without burst in. So in the Church Judas, etc., *as far as* then shall the wind and the storm cease, Jesus sitting and reigning in the ship, which is the universal Church.

*They went away in the desert. ((BEDA.))* By seeking solitude he tries the faith of the crowds, whether it follows him, and having tried it he rewards it with a worthy recompense. But the crowds, not with beasts of burden, not with carriages, but by the very labour of their feet, take up the journey of the desert, and show their desire of salvation. Again, by receiving the weary, by teaching the ignorant, by healing the sick, by refreshing the fasting, he intimates how much he is delighted by the devotion of them that believe.

*And on foot.* Note that they did not come to the other bank of the sea without a sailing of the Jordan. But, some strait or lake being passed over, they went to the nearest places of the same region, whither even the natives on foot were able to come.

*And he had compassion. ((BEDA.))* How he had compassion Matthew sets forth more fully in this manner: *And he had compassion on them, and healed their infirmities.* For this is truly to have compassion on the poor and on them that have no shepherd, and to open the way of truth, and the languishing to heal, and by refreshing the fasting to hearten them to the praise of the heavenly bounty; and the things that follow declare that he did this.

Hail to the Lord's Anointed, great David's greater Son

echoes.text: For what great nation is there, that has a god so near to them, as Yahweh our God is whenever we call on him?
echoes.note: 'Without God in the world,' contrasted with Israel's nearness, inverts Moses' boast that no nation has a god so near as YHWH is to Israel. The privilege of covenantal nearness sets up the Gentiles' former exclusion.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.” God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This […]
echoes.note: The contrast of 'circumcision'/'uncircumcision' and 'the covenants of the promise' draws on the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision and its promises. This is the OT institution Paul presupposes when defining Gentile alienation 'in the flesh.'

echoes.text: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Get out of your country, and from your relatives, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you. I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
echoes.note: 'Strangers from the covenants of the promise' presupposes the Abrahamic promise of blessing and land. The 'promise' Gentiles were excluded from is the recurrent patriarchal covenant promise, the availability of which frames their reincorporation.

echoes.text: He shows his word to Jacob; his statutes and his ordinances to Israel. He has not done this for just any nation. They don’t know his ordinances. Praise Yah!
echoes.note: 'He has not dealt thus with any other nation; they do not know his ordinances' parallels the Gentiles being 'without God,' aliens to Israel's covenant privileges. The thematic coherence is strong though unmarked.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: 'You who once were far off are made near' draws directly on Isaiah's 'Peace, peace, to the far and to the near.' The far/near pairing is the controlling OT text here, used both at 2:13 and quoted at 2:17, and its volume and recurrence make it the structural backbone of the pericope.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The bringing 'near' of those far off anticipates the herald-of-peace announcement Paul evokes more fully at 2:17. The Zion-restoration framework of Isaiah 52 coheres with the reconciliation theme of 'made near in the blood.'

echoes.text: Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of face, as at this day; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, who are near, and who are far off, through all the countries where you have driven them, because of their trespass that they have trespassed against you.
echoes.note: 'Those near and those far off' as a merism for all Israel/the scattered resonates with Paul's far/near language. The phrase is a stock OT idiom for the dispersed, lending availability to Paul's spatial reconciliation imagery.

echoes.text: For to us a child is born. To us a son is given; and the government will be on his shoulders. His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on the throne of David, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will perform this.
echoes.note: 'He is our peace' resonates with the messianic 'Prince of Peace' whose government brings unending peace. The identification of the Messiah personally with peace coheres strongly with Isaiah's peace-bringing royal child.

echoes.text: He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land, and when he marches through our fortresses, then we will raise against him seven shepherds, and eight leaders of men.
echoes.note: 'This one shall be peace' (of the Bethlehem ruler) parallels 'he is our peace.' Micah's messianic peace-figure offers an available OT precedent for predicating peace of the Messiah himself.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The making of peace and proclamation context underlying 'making peace' anticipates the explicit herald citation at 2:17. The peace-establishment theme coheres with the Isaianic good-news-of-peace background.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: 'Preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near' quotes 'Peace, peace, to the far and to the near.' The double 'peace' and the far/near pair are reproduced verbatim in sense, making this the clearest formal citation in the chapter.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: 'He came and preached peace' evokes the herald 'who publishes peace, who brings good news' of Zion's restoration. The act of proclaiming peace (euangelizo eirenen) blends Isaiah 52:7's gospel-herald with 57:19's far/near, a conflated allusion Paul builds his reconciliation climax upon.

echoes.text: I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow will be cut off; and he will speak peace to the nations: and his dominion will be from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.
echoes.note: The messianic king 'shall speak peace to the nations,' his rule reaching far, parallels Christ preaching peace to far and near. The Gentile-inclusive scope of Zechariah's peace-proclamation coheres with Paul's two-group reconciliation.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Access in one Spirit to the Father' resonates with the Spirit of the LORD resting on the messianic shoot, mediating divine presence. The Spirit-mediated approach to God coheres faintly with Isaiah's endowment of the Spirit, though no verbal tie exists.

echoes.text: He shall take a censer full of coals of fire from off the altar before Yahweh, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the veil: and he shall put the incense on the fire before Yahweh, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is on the testimony, so that he will not die. He shall take some of the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he […]
echoes.note: 'Access' to the Father reworks the cultic restriction of approach into God's presence, granted now to both groups by the Spirit. The Day of Atonement's controlled access supplies the figural temple-approach background reconciliation overturns.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: 'Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone' draws on 'I lay in Zion a stone, a tested cornerstone, a precious foundation.' Isaiah 28:16 is a recurrent NT messianic stone-text; its foundation/cornerstone vocabulary directly supplies Paul's temple-building imagery.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: The 'chief cornerstone' (akrogoniaios/kephale gonias) echoes 'the stone the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.' The widely-used messianic stone testimonium coheres with the cornerstone designation, though Paul's primary stone-text here is Isaiah 28:16.

echoes.text: Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.
echoes.note: 'A habitation of God in the Spirit' / 'holy temple' echoes the sanctuary command 'let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.' God's indwelling of a built structure is the controlling OT temple-presence theme Paul transfers to the church.

echoes.text: It came to pass, when the priests had come out of the holy place, that the cloud filled Yahweh’s house, so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for Yahweh’s glory filled Yahweh’s house. Then Solomon said, “Yahweh has said that he would dwell in the thick darkness. I have surely built you a house of habitation, a place for you to dwell in forever.”
echoes.note: 'Growing into a holy temple... a habitation of God' evokes the glory filling Solomon's temple as God's dwelling place. The temple-as-divine-residence motif coheres directly with believers as God's new dwelling by the Spirit.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: 'My dwelling place shall be with them... I will be their God' parallels the church as 'a habitation of God in the Spirit.' Ezekiel's eschatological-covenant dwelling, joined to Spirit-language, coheres with Paul's Spirit-indwelt temple.

echoes.text: In that day, this song will be sung in the land of Judah: “We have a strong city. God appoints salvation for walls and bulwarks. Open the gates, that the righteous nation may enter: the one which keeps faith.
echoes.note: 'Fellow citizens with the saints' and the strong, gate-opened city for the righteous nation resonate with the temple-city imagery. The citizenship-in-God's-city motif coheres faintly with Isaiah's Zion-city of salvation.

echoes.text: and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple; even he shall build Yahweh’s temple; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule on his throne; and he shall be a priest on his throne; and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.
echoes.note: 'The Branch... shall build the temple of the LORD' resonates with Christ as cornerstone of a growing holy temple. The messianic temple-builder oracle coheres with Christ being the foundation of the new sanctuary.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses prays for a successor so Israel will not be 'as sheep which have no shepherd,' the precise phrase Mark applies to the crowd. Jesus stepping in to teach is cast as the Moses-appointed shepherd over a leaderless people. Verbal correspondence and thematic coherence make this a strong allusion.

echoes.text: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’”
echoes.note: Micaiah sees Israel 'scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd' because their king-shepherd has failed. With Herod's failure as shepherd-king just narrated, Mark's shepherdless-sheep description points pointedly to this text. Strong verbal and thematic fit.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.
echoes.note: Ezekiel indicts Israel's shepherds and says the flock was 'scattered, because there was no shepherd,' promising that God himself will shepherd them. Jesus' compassion and teaching enact Yahweh's promised shepherding of the abandoned flock. High thematic coherence with the immediately preceding failure of Herod.

echoes.text: For the teraphim have spoken vanity, and the diviners have seen a lie; and they have told false dreams. They comfort in vain. Therefore they go their way like sheep. They are oppressed, because there is no shepherd.
echoes.note: The people 'wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd' because false guidance has failed them. Mark's shepherdless crowd resonates with Zechariah's diagnosis. Verbal overlap on the shepherdless-sheep image supports a solid allusion, though Numbers/Ezekiel are nearer.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: The leader is to 'go out before them and come in before them,' guiding their movements, language Mark's narrative of the crowd's pursuit and Jesus' going-out-to-teach faintly mirrors. Reinforces the Moses-successor framing of v.34. Contested as a secondary layer of the same Numbers context.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: Woe to shepherds who scatter the flock; God will gather his scattered sheep and raise true shepherds. The shepherdless crowd that Jesus gathers and teaches coheres with this oracle of regathering. Recurrence of the false-shepherd/true-shepherd theme strengthens the echo.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening. When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he did to the people, he said, “What is this thing that you do for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning to evening?” Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God. When they have a matter, they come to me, and I judge […]
echoes.note: Moses is so pressed by the people seeking him that he has no respite, prompting Jethro's counsel to share the load. The crowds giving Jesus and the Twelve 'no leisure so much as to eat' faintly recalls the overburdened-mediator scene. Contested, thematic only.

notes.text: That feed — They are said to have fed this people, because it was their duty so to do.

Behold — Even the Jewish doctors, as well as the Christian interpreters, understand this as a prophecy of the Messiah who is called the branch, Isaiah iv, 2; liii, 2. And here, he is called the righteous branch, not only because himself was righteous, but because he maketh his people righteous. Shall execute - Protecting the innocent, and defending his people throughout the world, judging the prince of the world, and by his spirit governing his people.

Judah — During the reign and kingdom of the Messiah the people of God typified by Judah and Israel shall be saved with a spiritual salvation, and God will be a special protection to them. And this - The name wherewith this branch shall be called, shall be, The Lord our righteousness. This place is an eminent proof of the Godhead of Christ, he is here called Jehovah, and what is proper to God alone, namely to justify, is here applied to Christ. He who knew no sin, was made sin, (that is, a sacrifice for sin) for us, that we might be made, the righteousness of God in him.

glossa.text: *Woe to the pastors,* etc. ((HIER.)) Because all hope of the Jewish kingdom has failed, he passes over to the princes of the Church; and, the synagogue with its own pastors being forsaken and condemned, the word is made to the apostles, of whom it is said, *I will raise up over them pastors ((Ezech. XXXIV))*, etc.

*Behold the days come, saith,* etc. ((ID.)) The pastors of the synagogue being cast off, that is to say the Scribes and the Pharisees, and the apostles being put in their place, Christ the pastor of pastors is brought in.

notes.text: Lie down — To repose myself at noon, as the manner was in those hot countries. Green - Where there is both delight and plenty of provisions.
Restoreth — Hebrew. He bringeth it back; from its errors and wandering. For - Not for any worth in me, but for the glory of his justice, and faithfulness, and goodness.
Thy rod and thy staff — Two words denoting the same thing, and both designing God's pastoral care over him.

A table — Thou furnishest me with plenty of provisions and comforts. Oil - With aromatic ointments, which were then used at great feasts; thy comforts delight my soul. Runneth over - Thou hast given me a plentiful portions, signified by the cup, given to the guests by the master of the feast. This psalm is generally thought to have been composed by David, upon bringing the ark of God from the house of Obed- edom, into the tabernacle which David had built for it, 2 Sam. vi, 12, 17. Wherein he hath a farther prospect to the temple, which he earnestly desired and intended to build. Moreover because the tabernacle, and temple, and ark, were types of Christ, and of his church and of heaven. David extended his thoughts to them also, or at least the Holy Ghost designed to comprehend them under these typical expressions. He shews God's sovereignty over the world, ver. 1, 2. Who shall receive his blessing, ver. 3-6. An exhortation to receive Christ, ver. 7-10. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* ((CASS.)) The Prophet foretold the return of the people from Babylon. *The Lord ruleth me.* A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, that all may hope in the mercy of God. ((AUG.)) The Church speaks of Christ.

*In a place of pasture.* ((CASS.)) The first grace, a place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate upon it. *Upon the water.* The second grace, the water of refreshment.

*My soul.* ((ID.)) The third grace, etc., *as far as* but first he brought me up upon the water of refreshment, first he converted my soul. *He hath led.* ((ID.)) The fourth, in that he led me upon the precepts of charity. *Upon the paths.* ((AUG.)) The narrower commandments and the more perfect counsels; as it were upon paths few just men walk, even as paths are narrower than roads.

*For though I shall walk.* ((CASS.)) The fifth, that in the shadow of death he fears no evils. *Thou art with me.* ((AUG.)) In the heart by faith, that after the shadow of death I may be with thee. *Thy rod.* ((CASS.)) The sixth, correction; or the rod is strictness, which converts vices. The staff is governance, which upholds the faithful.

*Thou hast prepared in my sight.* ((CASS.)) The seventh, the table of the Lord, the blessed banqueting, the fullness of faith, the heavenly food, of which the Apostle: *He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself. In my sight a table:* even if not that of the wicked. Of this it is said: *But these at the table of the rich man,* that is, of Christ, *know that thou too must prepare the like,* that is, to suffer as he did. *Thou hast anointed:* the eighth, the anointing of the head, namely of Christ, which was dried up by no barrenness of sin, whence the rest of the members rejoice, because from the head the ointment ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and unto the skirt of his garment. *And my chalice.* The ninth, the chalice, the blood of Christ, which so inebriates that it makes men sober. *Mine,* because I receive it. Or, thine, because thou givest it. The table and the chalice, flesh and blood, although they are one sacrament, yet under diverse species, because both are taken, are here set down separately.
*And mercy.* ((CASS.)) The tenth, mercy following after unto keeping, which goes before unto the conferring of grace.
*And that I may dwell.* ((HIER.)) This is joined to all the things above. As though: thou hast placed, thou hast brought up, thou hast led, etc., and this to the end that I may dwell.

notes.text: Wherefore remember — Such a remembrance strengthens faith, and increases gratitude. That ye being formerly gentiles in the flesh - Neither circumcised in body nor in spirit. Who were accordingly called the uncircumcision - By way of reproach. By that which is called the circumcision - By those who call themselves the circumcised, and think this a proof that they are the people of God; and who indeed have that outward circumcision which is performed by hands in the flesh.

Were at that time without Christ — Having no faith in, or knowledge of, him. Being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel - Both as to their temporal privileges and spiritual blessings. And strangers to the covenants of promise - The great promise in both the Jewish and Christian covenant was the Messiah. Having no hope - Because they had no promise whereon to ground their hope. And being without God - Wholly ignorant of the true God, and so in effect atheists. Such in truth are, more or less, all men, in all ages, till they know God by the teaching of his own Spirit. In the world - The wide, vain world, wherein ye wandered up and down, unholy and unhappy.
Far off — From God and his people. Nigh - Intimately united to both.

For he is our peace — Not only as he purchased it, but as he is the very bond and center of union. He who hath made both - Jews and gentiles, one church. The apostle describes,

1. The conjunction of the gentiles with Israel, ver. 14, 15. And,

2. The conjunction of both with God, ver. 15-18. Each description is subdivided into two parts. And the former part of the one, concerning abolishing the enmity, answers the former part of the other; the latter part of the one, concerning the evangelical decrees, the latter part of the other. And hath broken down the middle wall of partition - Alluding to that wall of old, which separated the court of Israel from the court of the gentiles. Such a wall was the ceremonial law, which Christ had now taken away.

15. Having abolished by his suffering in the flesh the cause of enmity between the Jews and gentiles, even the law of ceremonial commandments, through his decrees - Which offer mercy to all; see Colossians ii, 14. That he might form the two - Jew and gentile. Into one new man - one mystical body.
In one body — One church. Having slain - By his own death on the cross. The enmity - Which had been between sinners and God.

And he came — After his resurrection. And preached peace - By his ministers and his Spirit. To you - Gentiles. That were afar off - At the utmost distance from God. And to them that were nigh - To the Jews, who were comparatively nigh, being his visible church.

For through him, we both — Jews and gentiles. Have access - Liberty of approaching, by the guidance and aid of one Spirit to God as our Father. Christ, the Spirit, and the Father, the three-one God, stand frequently in the same order.
Therefore ye are no longer strangers, but citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem; no longer foreigners, but received into the very family of God.

And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets — As the foundation sustains the building, so the word of God, declared by the apostles and prophets, sustains the faith of all believers. God laid the foundation by them; but Christ himself is the chief corner-stone of the foundation. Elsewhere he is termed the foundation itself, 1 Cor. iii, 11.

On whom all the building fitly framed together — The whole fabric of the universal church rises up like a great pile of living materials. Into an holy temple in the Lord - Dedicated to Christ, and inhabited by him, in which he displays his presence, and is worshipped and glorified. What is the temple of Diana of the Ephesians, whom ye formerly worshipped, to this?

glossa.text: *For which cause.* That you may know that all things are from the grace of God. He had compared the Jews and the Gentiles, in that both had been under sin, now he shows that the Gentiles were the more unworthy and had endured the reproaches of the Jews, so that, being now equal to the Jews, they may be the more beholden to the grace of God. *Sometime you.* In certain codices it is found to be written: *who,* in this place: *you who were Gentiles,* and according to this it is read suspensively as far as this place: *Now, however, in Christ,* etc.; the sense nevertheless remaining the same.

*Strangers.* Hospes, as it were ostii pes, the foot of the door, because when one was received into a house, the master of the house, and he who was received, set his foot upon the doorway, and, right hands having been given, he swore that his entry was peaceable.

*Who hath made both one.* For he himself is the corner stone, in whom two peoples, as walls coming to one another from a different angle, are joined as it were in the kiss of peace. *The wall.* That is, the obstacle, on this side from the law, on that side from idolatry.

*Making peace,* etc. He makes peace between them, that he may reconcile both to God the Father. *In himself.* Not otherwise than by the cross, that is, by death, did he slay the enmity which was between God and men, that is, he forgave sins. For the death of the Saviour profited all.
*You were far off,* etc. If thou lovest God with affection, thou art near: if thou hatest, thou art far off. For it is not by regions that anyone is far from God, but by affections.

*You are not strangers.* That is, less worthy in the faith, as those formerly received under the law. *And sojourners.* That is, foreign to God. *But you are fellow citizens.* That is, of the same right and dignity in the house of God. *Of the saints.* Not of carnal Israel. *And the domestics.* That is, of the household. *Of God.* To whom he reveals secrets.

*He himself the chief corner stone,* etc. ((AUG., in Psal. LXXXVI.)) Lest the Apostles or the prophets (in whom the city is founded) should hold to themselves, following on he says in himself: *He himself the chief corner stone, Christ Jesus;* for indeed the whole building rests upon Christ as upon the first foundation: which foundation is at the top, not at the bottom, as in a bodily structure.
*It groweth into a holy temple in the Lord.* No one is so perfect that he cannot grow.

notes.text: Luke ix, 10.
Matt. xiv, 13; John vi, 1.
They departed — Across a creek or corner of the lake.
Coming out — of the vessel.

glossa.text:
*And gathering together. ((HIER.))* To the place whence the rivers go out they return. They always render thanks to God for those things which they have received.

*All things.* The apostles report to the Lord not only what they themselves had done and taught, but also what John suffered while they were teaching. Either his own disciples, or those of the same John, as Matthew writes.

*Come apart. ((BEDA.))* Not only for the sake of a seeking again, but mystically it signifies that, Judaea being left, which, etc., *as far as* he comes apart, he leads those whom he chooses, that among men living ill they may not attend to evil things, as Lot in Sodom, and Job in the land of Hus, and Abdias in the house of Achab.

*Rest ye.* As the birds in the branches of the mustard. Little is the rest here for the saints, long the labour: but afterwards it is said to them that they should rest from their labours.

*For there were,* etc. ((HIER.)) In the ark of Noe the animals that were within were sent forth, and those that were without burst in. So in the Church Judas, etc., *as far as* then shall the wind and the storm cease, Jesus sitting and reigning in the ship, which is the universal Church.

*They went away in the desert. ((BEDA.))* By seeking solitude he tries the faith of the crowds, whether it follows him, and having tried it he rewards it with a worthy recompense. But the crowds, not with beasts of burden, not with carriages, but by the very labour of their feet, take up the journey of the desert, and show their desire of salvation. Again, by receiving the weary, by teaching the ignorant, by healing the sick, by refreshing the fasting, he intimates how much he is delighted by the devotion of them that believe.

*And on foot.* Note that they did not come to the other bank of the sea without a sailing of the Jordan. But, some strait or lake being passed over, they went to the nearest places of the same region, whither even the natives on foot were able to come.

*And he had compassion. ((BEDA.))* How he had compassion Matthew sets forth more fully in this manner: *And he had compassion on them, and healed their infirmities.* For this is truly to have compassion on the poor and on them that have no shepherd, and to open the way of truth, and the languishing to heal, and by refreshing the fasting to hearten them to the praise of the heavenly bounty; and the things that follow declare that he did this.

echoes.text: For what great nation is there, that has a god so near to them, as Yahweh our God is whenever we call on him?
echoes.note: 'Without God in the world,' contrasted with Israel's nearness, inverts Moses' boast that no nation has a god so near as YHWH is to Israel. The privilege of covenantal nearness sets up the Gentiles' former exclusion.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.” God said to Abraham, “As for you, you will keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This […]
echoes.note: The contrast of 'circumcision'/'uncircumcision' and 'the covenants of the promise' draws on the Abrahamic covenant of circumcision and its promises. This is the OT institution Paul presupposes when defining Gentile alienation 'in the flesh.'

echoes.text: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Get out of your country, and from your relatives, and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you. I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who curses you. All of the families of the earth will be blessed in you.”
echoes.note: 'Strangers from the covenants of the promise' presupposes the Abrahamic promise of blessing and land. The 'promise' Gentiles were excluded from is the recurrent patriarchal covenant promise, the availability of which frames their reincorporation.

echoes.text: He shows his word to Jacob; his statutes and his ordinances to Israel. He has not done this for just any nation. They don’t know his ordinances. Praise Yah!
echoes.note: 'He has not dealt thus with any other nation; they do not know his ordinances' parallels the Gentiles being 'without God,' aliens to Israel's covenant privileges. The thematic coherence is strong though unmarked.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: 'You who once were far off are made near' draws directly on Isaiah's 'Peace, peace, to the far and to the near.' The far/near pairing is the controlling OT text here, used both at 2:13 and quoted at 2:17, and its volume and recurrence make it the structural backbone of the pericope.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The bringing 'near' of those far off anticipates the herald-of-peace announcement Paul evokes more fully at 2:17. The Zion-restoration framework of Isaiah 52 coheres with the reconciliation theme of 'made near in the blood.'

echoes.text: Lord, righteousness belongs to you, but to us confusion of face, as at this day; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, who are near, and who are far off, through all the countries where you have driven them, because of their trespass that they have trespassed against you.
echoes.note: 'Those near and those far off' as a merism for all Israel/the scattered resonates with Paul's far/near language. The phrase is a stock OT idiom for the dispersed, lending availability to Paul's spatial reconciliation imagery.

echoes.text: For to us a child is born. To us a son is given; and the government will be on his shoulders. His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace there shall be no end, on the throne of David, and on his kingdom, to establish it, and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from that time on, even forever. The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will perform this.
echoes.note: 'He is our peace' resonates with the messianic 'Prince of Peace' whose government brings unending peace. The identification of the Messiah personally with peace coheres strongly with Isaiah's peace-bringing royal child.

echoes.text: He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land, and when he marches through our fortresses, then we will raise against him seven shepherds, and eight leaders of men.
echoes.note: 'This one shall be peace' (of the Bethlehem ruler) parallels 'he is our peace.' Micah's messianic peace-figure offers an available OT precedent for predicating peace of the Messiah himself.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The making of peace and proclamation context underlying 'making peace' anticipates the explicit herald citation at 2:17. The peace-establishment theme coheres with the Isaianic good-news-of-peace background.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: 'Preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near' quotes 'Peace, peace, to the far and to the near.' The double 'peace' and the far/near pair are reproduced verbatim in sense, making this the clearest formal citation in the chapter.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: 'He came and preached peace' evokes the herald 'who publishes peace, who brings good news' of Zion's restoration. The act of proclaiming peace (euangelizo eirenen) blends Isaiah 52:7's gospel-herald with 57:19's far/near, a conflated allusion Paul builds his reconciliation climax upon.

echoes.text: I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow will be cut off; and he will speak peace to the nations: and his dominion will be from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth.
echoes.note: The messianic king 'shall speak peace to the nations,' his rule reaching far, parallels Christ preaching peace to far and near. The Gentile-inclusive scope of Zechariah's peace-proclamation coheres with Paul's two-group reconciliation.

echoes.text: The Spirit of Yahweh will rest on him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Access in one Spirit to the Father' resonates with the Spirit of the LORD resting on the messianic shoot, mediating divine presence. The Spirit-mediated approach to God coheres faintly with Isaiah's endowment of the Spirit, though no verbal tie exists.

echoes.text: He shall take a censer full of coals of fire from off the altar before Yahweh, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the veil: and he shall put the incense on the fire before Yahweh, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat that is on the testimony, so that he will not die. He shall take some of the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it with his finger on the mercy seat on the east; and before the mercy seat he […]
echoes.note: 'Access' to the Father reworks the cultic restriction of approach into God's presence, granted now to both groups by the Spirit. The Day of Atonement's controlled access supplies the figural temple-approach background reconciliation overturns.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: 'Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone' draws on 'I lay in Zion a stone, a tested cornerstone, a precious foundation.' Isaiah 28:16 is a recurrent NT messianic stone-text; its foundation/cornerstone vocabulary directly supplies Paul's temple-building imagery.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: The 'chief cornerstone' (akrogoniaios/kephale gonias) echoes 'the stone the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.' The widely-used messianic stone testimonium coheres with the cornerstone designation, though Paul's primary stone-text here is Isaiah 28:16.

echoes.text: Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.
echoes.note: 'A habitation of God in the Spirit' / 'holy temple' echoes the sanctuary command 'let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.' God's indwelling of a built structure is the controlling OT temple-presence theme Paul transfers to the church.

echoes.text: It came to pass, when the priests had come out of the holy place, that the cloud filled Yahweh’s house, so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for Yahweh’s glory filled Yahweh’s house. Then Solomon said, “Yahweh has said that he would dwell in the thick darkness. I have surely built you a house of habitation, a place for you to dwell in forever.”
echoes.note: 'Growing into a holy temple... a habitation of God' evokes the glory filling Solomon's temple as God's dwelling place. The temple-as-divine-residence motif coheres directly with believers as God's new dwelling by the Spirit.

echoes.text: My tent also shall be with them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
echoes.note: 'My dwelling place shall be with them... I will be their God' parallels the church as 'a habitation of God in the Spirit.' Ezekiel's eschatological-covenant dwelling, joined to Spirit-language, coheres with Paul's Spirit-indwelt temple.

echoes.text: In that day, this song will be sung in the land of Judah: “We have a strong city. God appoints salvation for walls and bulwarks. Open the gates, that the righteous nation may enter: the one which keeps faith.
echoes.note: 'Fellow citizens with the saints' and the strong, gate-opened city for the righteous nation resonate with the temple-city imagery. The citizenship-in-God's-city motif coheres faintly with Isaiah's Zion-city of salvation.

echoes.text: and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple; even he shall build Yahweh’s temple; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule on his throne; and he shall be a priest on his throne; and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.
echoes.note: 'The Branch... shall build the temple of the LORD' resonates with Christ as cornerstone of a growing holy temple. The messianic temple-builder oracle coheres with Christ being the foundation of the new sanctuary.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: Moses prays for a successor so Israel will not be 'as sheep which have no shepherd,' the precise phrase Mark applies to the crowd. Jesus stepping in to teach is cast as the Moses-appointed shepherd over a leaderless people. Verbal correspondence and thematic coherence make this a strong allusion.

echoes.text: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. Yahweh said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’”
echoes.note: Micaiah sees Israel 'scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd' because their king-shepherd has failed. With Herod's failure as shepherd-king just narrated, Mark's shepherdless-sheep description points pointedly to this text. Strong verbal and thematic fit.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.
echoes.note: Ezekiel indicts Israel's shepherds and says the flock was 'scattered, because there was no shepherd,' promising that God himself will shepherd them. Jesus' compassion and teaching enact Yahweh's promised shepherding of the abandoned flock. High thematic coherence with the immediately preceding failure of Herod.

echoes.text: For the teraphim have spoken vanity, and the diviners have seen a lie; and they have told false dreams. They comfort in vain. Therefore they go their way like sheep. They are oppressed, because there is no shepherd.
echoes.note: The people 'wander like sheep; they are afflicted for lack of a shepherd' because false guidance has failed them. Mark's shepherdless crowd resonates with Zechariah's diagnosis. Verbal overlap on the shepherdless-sheep image supports a solid allusion, though Numbers/Ezekiel are nearer.

echoes.text: “Let Yahweh, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of Yahweh not be as sheep which have no shepherd.”
echoes.note: The leader is to 'go out before them and come in before them,' guiding their movements, language Mark's narrative of the crowd's pursuit and Jesus' going-out-to-teach faintly mirrors. Reinforces the Moses-successor framing of v.34. Contested as a secondary layer of the same Numbers context.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: Woe to shepherds who scatter the flock; God will gather his scattered sheep and raise true shepherds. The shepherdless crowd that Jesus gathers and teaches coheres with this oracle of regathering. Recurrence of the false-shepherd/true-shepherd theme strengthens the echo.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening. When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he did to the people, he said, “What is this thing that you do for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning to evening?” Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God. When they have a matter, they come to me, and I judge […]
echoes.note: Moses is so pressed by the people seeking him that he has no respite, prompting Jethro's counsel to share the load. The crowds giving Jesus and the Twelve 'no leisure so much as to eat' faintly recalls the overburdened-mediator scene. Contested, thematic only.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Come away to a deserted place and rest a while.
Even here we are gathered to the heart of God.
The crowd was like sheep without a shepherd.
And he had compassion, and began to teach.
I will not take my steadfast love from you, says the Lord.
Your covenant stands firm; your mercy never ends.
Come, all you weary; come, let us worship.
We come away to rest in God. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: You have given and given until there was no time even to eat; the Shepherd knows, and says: come away by yourselves to a quiet place.
Come away and rest a while.
But the crowds run ahead around the lake, hungry and lost like sheep without a shepherd, and his heart breaks open with compassion.
Come away and rest a while.
This is the steadfast love God swore to David: a love that will not be taken back, firm as the heavens, sure as the dawn.
Come away and rest a while.
So bring your tiredness here; wherever he goes, the sick are laid in the marketplace just to touch the edge of his cloak and be healed.
Come away and rest a while, for the Shepherd is here.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Come to a quiet place; lay your burdens down.
Come away and rest a while.
He saw the crowds and had compassion on them.
Come away and rest a while.
God's steadfast love will never be taken away.
Come away and rest a while.
Come, all you weary; come, let us worship.
Come away and rest a while. Amen.
